beats.text: Every time you open Claude, you explain the same things again.
How you like your work done. What to avoid. What format you want.
A skill fixes that.
It is one small file. Claude reads it, and follows it, every time.
In the next ten minutes, you will build one from scratch.
You will test it on a real task, and download a finished one to keep.
The link is in the description.
A skill is a folder with one file in it.
The file is called SKILL dot M D.
At the top is a name, and a one line description.
Below that, plain instructions, written like a checklist.
Claude reads only the description at first.
That keeps things light. Many skills can sit there, and only the one that matches is loaded in full.
When your request matches it, Claude loads the full instructions, and follows them.
There is no code. There are no plugins to install.
If you can write a checklist, you can write a skill.
Here is what we are building: a skill called post autopsy.
You give it your social post stats.
It tells you which posts flopped, why, and what to change.
Skills live in one of two places.
Personal skills go in dot claude, then skills, inside your home folder. They work in every project.
Project skills go in dot claude, then skills, inside one project folder. Anyone who opens that project gets them.
We will make a personal one.
Step one. Make the folder.
Open your terminal, and go to your Claude skills folder.
On most setups, that is dot claude, then skills, inside your home folder.
On Windows, it is the dot claude folder inside your user folder. Same name, same layout.
Make a new folder called post autopsy, with M K dir.
Then C D into it.
Now create an empty file named SKILL dot M D.
That is the whole setup. A folder, and one file.
You can also ask Claude Code to create it for you. But doing it by hand once shows you how simple it is.
Here is how it looks on disk.
One folder named after the skill. One file inside it.
Step two. Write the description.
Open SKILL dot M D in any text editor.
The file starts with three dashes, then two fields.
The first field is name. Ours is post autopsy, all lowercase, with a dash.
Lowercase letters, numbers, and dashes only. No spaces.
The second field is description, and it is the most important line in the file.
The description is the trigger. It tells Claude when to use the skill.
So write what the skill does, and when to use it.
Ours says: reads your social post stats, and tells you which posts flopped, why, and what to change.
Then a second sentence: use when the user shares post analytics.
Close the block with three more dashes.
Be specific. A vague description is the number one reason a skill never fires.
Helps with posts. That tells Claude nothing.
Reads post stats, and says which posts flopped and why. Use when the user shares analytics. That is a trigger.
Use the words you would actually say. Post stats. Analytics. Why is this not working.
Those are the phrases Claude matches your request against.
Keep it to one or two sentences.
Step three. Write the steps.
Under the front matter, add a heading with the skill name.
Then a section called steps, with a numbered list.
Step one: find the median views across all the posts.
The median is the middle value, so one viral post cannot skew the picture.
Here is why. Say nine posts get four hundred views, and one gets forty thousand.
The average says four thousand three hundred sixty. The median says four hundred, which is what a normal post does.
Step two: sort the posts into hits and misses. Hits are above the median. Misses are below it.
Step three: look for patterns, using only the data. Length, topic, format, and posting day.
Step four: give three changes, and tie each one to evidence from the posts.
That last step matters most. Compare two answers.
One says, post more often.
The other says, posts with a number in the title averaged four thousand four hundred views.
Only the second one is something you can check.
Now add a section called rules.
Rule one: use only the numbers I give you.
Rule two: keep the answer under three hundred words.
Rules are where your guardrails go. Anything you keep correcting by hand belongs here.
Notice the style. Every line is short, concrete, and testable.
You could check any one of them, and say yes, it did that, or no, it did not.
If a line is fuzzy, like make it good, Claude has nothing to follow.
Rewrite it until you could check it.
Save the file. That is the entire skill.
Step four. Test it on a real task.
Open Claude Code in any folder.
Paste in ten of your own posts, with their view counts.
Here is a sample. Ten posts, one line each: the title, then the views.
Now type: run a post autopsy.
Watch what Claude does. It should tell you it loaded the skill.
Here is the result. Median views: one thousand seven hundred sixty.
Five hits, five misses.
The pattern: every hit promises something specific. A number, a result, or a free thing.
Every miss is a vague update, with no promise in it.
Then three changes, each with the numbers behind it.
If nothing happens, do not guess. Ask Claude: what skills do you have available?
It lists every skill it can see.
If post autopsy is missing, the folder is in the wrong place, or the three dashes at the top are broken.
If it is listed, but never fires, your description is too vague. Go back to step two.
Now be a tough reviewer. Does it follow the steps, in order? Did it invent any number?
Check the averages. The hits average four thousand four hundred sixty views.
The misses average five hundred fourteen.
Both are right. Every number traces back to the ten posts you pasted.
But say it had made up a number. Maybe a click rate you never gave it.
Do not rewrite the whole skill. Add one line to the rules.
Never invent numbers. If a number is missing, say so.
Save, and run it again.
Skills get good by testing, not by writing more.
Then break it on purpose.
Paste only three posts. Paste a post with zero views. Paste a messy list with extra text in it.
Each one shows you a rule you forgot to write.
Step five. Make it better. Three upgrades.
Upgrade one: add an example of a good answer.
Claude copies the shape and the tone of an example far better than it follows a description of them.
Keep the example short. Three or four lines is enough.
Upgrade two: add a rule for what it should refuse.
Ours says: if I share fewer than five posts, say the sample is too small, and ask for more.
That one rule stops confident nonsense from a tiny sample.
Upgrade three: add a final question.
End every run by asking: which change do you want to test first?
Now every run ends with a next step, instead of just a report.
Save, and test again.
Use the same ten posts first. Then paste in only three.
With three, it should refuse, and ask for more. If it does, the rule works.
One more tip. Keep the file short.
If it grows past a few hundred lines, split it.
Put long reference material in a second file, in the same folder.
Then tell Claude, inside SKILL dot M D, when to open it.
The finished version of this skill is free. The link is in the description.
The finished one goes a little further. It sets a clear baseline for hits and misses, and shows a small table.
It rewrites your two worst titles, and warns you when the sample is small.
Download the zip, and unzip it.
Drop the folder, named post autopsy, into your skills folder.
Open Claude Code, and say: run a post autopsy.
If it does not run, check two things.
The folder name, and the three dashes at the top of the file.
If you added the folder while Claude Code was open, restart it once.
And if you use the Claude app instead of the terminal, zip the folder, and upload it under settings, capabilities, skills.
Quick recap.
One: make the folder, with one file named SKILL dot M D.
Two: write a description that says what it does, and when to use it.
Three: write short, numbered steps, and a few rules.
Four: test it on real data, and fix what breaks, one line at a time.
Five: add an example, a refusal rule, and a closing question.
That is the whole loop. Write, test, fix.
If you want the full set, I packaged six skills.
Hook lab. Caption rewrite. Weekly review. Content calendar. Repurpose to Shorts. And this one, post autopsy.
